CREATORS.summary: The people who make the ads split three ways in this era. The agency holding companies kept consolidating and kept losing the media-buying job: media planning and buying moved either into the client (82% of ANA members ran an in-house agency by 2023) or into the platform's own automation, and what agencies did keep they increasingly sold as principal media (buying inventory in bulk and reselling it at an undisclosed markup) rather than as a disclosed commission or fee. The 15% commission the era-1 agencies invented finished dying here: the ANA/K2 report of 2016 documented pervasive undisclosed rebates in US media buying, and the ANA's 2024 and 2026 principal-media studies found governance lagging adoption. Consolidation peaked on 2025-11-26 when Omnicom closed its acquisition of Interpublic, creating a roughly $25-26B-revenue holding company. Second, the platforms became creators: Performance Max and Advantage+ assemble the creative from an asset feed, and Meta said over one million advertisers used its generative-AI tools to build more than 15 million ads in a single month in 2025. Third, individual creators became a media channel in their own right - IAB/PwC put US creator advertising at about $37B in 2025, growing at roughly twice the market rate, with a projected $44B in 2026. The through-line: the entity that composes the ad is less and less a person paid by the advertiser, and more and more the seller's own model.

BUYERS.summary: Era 7's marginal new buyer class is the algorithmic buyer: an advertiser who no longer picks keywords, placements or audiences but hands a budget, a conversion goal and an asset feed to the seller's model. Performance Max (Google, 2021) and Advantage+ (Meta, 2022) are the canonical products; by 2025 roughly 71% of Google advertisers globally (about 75% in the US) ran Performance Max, and Meta's automated ad products were running at about a $60B annualised revenue rate. Underneath that sits the long tail the auction created in era 6 and industrialised here: Meta has publicly cited more than 10 million active advertisers, and more than 2 million US businesses advertising monthly. The other new buyer class is the brand buying its own retailer's shelf: retail and commerce media reached $63.4B of US internet ad revenue in 2025, and structurally this is trade-promotion and co-op money - the manufacturer money that has flowed through retailers for a century - changing pricing mechanism from a negotiated allowance to an auction. Political money grew into a cyclical shock all its own, $11.1B across the 2023-24 US cycle. And direct mail, the oldest measurable-response buyer, was still spending about $37.3B in 2024, even as USPS Marketing Mail volume fell from 99 billion pieces in FY2008 to 56.8 billion in FY2025 - the same dollars buying far fewer, better-targeted pieces.

national_brand.statement: National brand buyers - the advertisers who still buy reach rather than response - account for about 36.6 percent of US advertising spend in 2025, roughly $145.7B, concentrated in national linear TV, national CTV and video, magazines, national out-of-home and upper-funnel digital. This is the largest or joint-largest pool, and it replaces the record's earlier reading that brand money had become the smallest of the four.
national_brand.unit: percent of US advertising spend, 2025 (MAGNA media-owner rail, $398B, direct mail excluded)
national_brand.method: SOURCED BY: NO SOURCE. No compiler publishes a US national-brand advertising figure for any year after 2007. Partial free evidence exists only for 2008-2010 (Census SAS national/regional air time, grade A) and for newspapers to 2012 (NAA). The two instruments that would source the pool - Guideline/SMI agency billing data and MAGNA's National domain inside MG8 - are licensed and were not purchased. The pool is a construction and must stay one. RAIL: MAGNA media-owner advertising revenue, $398B for 2025 (digital pure players $294B + traditional media owners $104B, which sums exactly, so DIRECT MAIL IS OUT of this rail). All four pools are defined ex-direct-mail to match, which is the fix for the mechanical residual depression the era-7 verifier flagged: the superseded residual was computed with direct mail excluded from the denominator but present in two subtracted pools. RAIL SENSITIVITY EXCEEDS EVERY INTERVAL IN THIS SPLIT: IRS SOI corporate advertising deductions read $473,153m for 2022 against MAGNA's $325,000m, a $148B wedge that is overwhelmingly direct-response and retail money. Any chart of this split must name its rail in the axis label, not the footnote. || AGGREGATION: median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 39.7, reference-class 36.6, decomposition 32.9). No extremizing, because the lenses share an evidence base. Three routes survive de-duplication and only one is independent of the other pools - the weakest methodological position of the four pools, which is why this pool carries the widest interval. || ROUTE N-A, residual against the observed total, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.50 (0.50 / 0.45 / 0.55). $398B less local retail less classified less direct response, with direct mail excluded on BOTH sides of the subtraction. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENT: the pool subtracted as local retail is a buyer-class pool, not BIA's inventory-geography pool, which moves the residual UP by roughly 11pp; consistent direct-mail treatment moves it UP by roughly a further 6pp. Inherits every upstream error by construction. || ROUTE N-B, bottom-up impression-priced build from IAB's mutually exclusive FY2025 format partition plus MAGNA traditional media-owner revenue, less the local-bought leg, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.30 (0.50 / 0.30 / 0.30). PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENT: pricing basis is not buyer intent (IAB's own caveat) - a brand advertiser transacting on CPC lands in 'performance' and a direct-response advertiser buying guaranteed CPM lands in 'CPM'; the two errors partly offset and the net on this pool is estimated DOWN 2 to 4pp, carried in the interval rather than the central. NOT FULLY INDEPENDENT OF N-A: both consume the performance-priced share of US digital, and all three lenses said so, so their 1.0-1.4pp agreement understates uncertainty and does not set the interval. || ROUTE N-C, advertiser-stated brand-building share (WARC/Ebiquity), WEIGHT 0.00 in every lens, bound only. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: global panel to US population, -2 to -4pp; large-advertiser panel to whole market, missing millions of self-serve advertisers who are almost entirely performance, -5 to -10pp; the 9pp one-year swing is read as sample composition, so the two-year mean is used. Adjusted it reads national brand near 22 percent, about 15 points below the construction, and it is the ONLY genuinely independent instrument bearing on this pool. || NEAR-DUPLICATE DECLARED: the monitored-spend band from AdAge Leading National Advertisers produces no free value and is a bound, not a route. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. It is NOT drawn from route dispersion, which would be false precision given that N-A and N-B share an input; the lower end is where the independent survey rail sits and the upper end is where local retail's lower bound pushes the residual.

local_retail.statement: Local and retail buyers account for about 23.5 percent of US advertising spend in 2025, roughly $93.5B. The pool has been nominally flat for a quarter of a century across three compilers that share no inputs - Coen $95.8B in 2000, Coen $94.3B in 2007, BIA/Kelsey's SMB plus local brands $90.2B in 2015 - which inside a market that grew 60 percent is a mechanically declining share.
local_retail.unit: percent of US advertising spend, 2025 (MAGNA media-owner rail, $398B, direct mail excluded)
local_retail.method: SOURCED BY: NOT SOURCED AS A MONEY TYPE, which is why the grade falls from B to C. The source that carried the B grade - BIA's $169B US local advertising total - measures a different object: BIA's own published definition is all media selling access to LOCAL AUDIENCES to ALL advertiser types INCLUDING national and regional companies. That is geography of inventory, not class of buyer. What IS available, and is the hunt's largest free evidence upgrade, is BIA's own advertiser-type ratio, published in summary form at $116.4B regional-and-national marketers against $59.2B SMBs (SMB = 33.7 percent), corroborated by the independent BIA/Kelsey 2015 vintage at SMB $50.4B of a $140.7B local total (35.9 percent). That ratio grades B, but the derived 2025 pool needs a regional-tier allocation and a rail conversion on top of it, so the pool is C. RAIL: MAGNA media-owner advertising revenue, $398B for 2025 (digital pure players $294B + traditional media owners $104B, which sums exactly, so DIRECT MAIL IS OUT of this rail). All four pools are defined ex-direct-mail to match, which is the fix for the mechanical residual depression the era-7 verifier flagged: the superseded residual was computed with direct mail excluded from the denominator but present in two subtracted pools. RAIL SENSITIVITY EXCEEDS EVERY INTERVAL IN THIS SPLIT: IRS SOI corporate advertising deductions read $473,153m for 2022 against MAGNA's $325,000m, a $148B wedge that is overwhelmingly direct-response and retail money. Any chart of this split must name its rail in the axis label, not the footnote. || AGGREGATION: median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 19.6, reference-class 23.5, decomposition 23.9). No extremizing. This is the best-supported of the four pools methodologically - three genuinely independent routes, each run by all three lenses. || ROUTE L-A, BIA's own advertiser-type cut, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.40 (0.42 / 0.40 / 0.35). PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENT, and it is the decisive one: BIA's population is buyers-of-local-inventory, which includes national and regional companies, so the correction on the record is DOWN and large. SMB-share drift is measured rather than assumed, 35.9 percent (2015) to 33.7 percent (current), a 2.2pp decline over a decade. Local direct mail (about $3-3.8B on BIA's own stated 90/10 national/local rule) is removed to match the ex-direct-mail denominator, and the classified and vertical money BIA admits sits inside its PC/Laptop digital definition (about $2-3.5B) is reassigned to classified so the two pools are disjoint. THE OPEN JUDGEMENT: BIA lumps 'regional' with 'national', and the regional tier is local-retail money in the Coen/NAA sense; the lenses allocate 30, 40 and about 44 percent of that lump to local retail. At 0 percent the pool reads 14.3 percent, at 45 percent it reads 24.1 percent. This one parameter is the widest unverified step in era 7. NOTE: the two BIA vintages are ONE compiler, so L-A is one route across all three lenses. || ROUTE L-B, medium-by-medium buyer-side build from government and trade rails plus platform filings, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.38 (0.38 / 0.00 bound-only / 0.40). PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: TIME GAP - the Census SAS national/local split stops at reference year 2010 and RAB thins after 2021, so both are carried forward 4 to 15 years; radio's local share is stable across two independent readings five years apart (72.2 percent Census 2010, 74.1 percent RAB 2015), which bounds the drift small for that medium, while TV's assumed-flat 36-40 percent is the weakest link. SELLER-SIDE VERSUS BUYER-SIDE - the Census classifies who bought the time, not what the money was for, which correctly leaves national direct-response TV out of local. The platform local-bought shares (Meta about 32 percent of US, Google about 20 percent) are calibrated judgements, not measurements, and swing the route by about $15B. || ROUTE L-C, establishment count times category advertising intensity, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.20 (0.20 / 0.20 / 0.25). PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: SMB survey average revenue per advertiser captures websites, SEO, promotions and marketing services that sit OUTSIDE the media rail, direction down about 20 percent; the count-based approach misses local advertisers who buy only traditional media and never touch a self-serve platform, direction up about 10 percent; and SMB is not the same as local - a $2m-revenue direct-to-consumer brand buying nationally on Meta is national direct response. NEAR-DUPLICATES DECLARED: the three lenses' parameterisations differ (3.5m x $22k; 4.5m x $14k; 4.0m x about $24k) but are one route, and they converge on $62B, $63B and $63B for the SMB leg. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. Its width is definitional, not statistical: the regional-tier allocation alone spans it.

classified.statement: Classified buyers - individuals and businesses paying to list a job, a car, a home or an item - account for about 2.5 percent of US advertising spend in 2025, roughly $9.95B, essentially all of it placed with digital marketplaces and job boards. On a listings-inclusive reading the money type is nearer $21B, of which $12-16B sits outside every published advertising series.
classified.unit: percent of US advertising spend, 2025 (MAGNA media-owner rail, $398B, direct mail excluded)
classified.method: SOURCED BY: SOURCED FOR 2008-2021 AT GRADE A ON THREE INDEPENDENT LEGS - the hunt's main finding, which overturns the note that no modern source publishes this. (1) US Census Bureau Service Annual Survey, NAICS 511110, 'Breakdown of Revenue by Advertising Type: classified advertising', free, 2005-2021 with 2012 and 2022 suppressed: $8,087m (2008) falling to $1,978m (2021), a government probability survey independent of NAA, Coen, IAB, MAGNA and BIA. (2) The same survey's NAICS 511140 directory advertising space line, free, 2005-2020: $11,400m (2008) to $1,781m (2020), replacing the two trade blogs the record previously cited. (3) IAB/PwC's classifieds format line, free, with its own share to about 2016 and a stated dollar figure inside 'Other' to 2021, $3.2B (2008) to $5.3B (2021). Overlap test passes: NAA $5,030m against Census $4,840m for newspaper classified in 2011, a 3.9 percent gap. The 2008 anchor is fully grade A at $22.7B. NOT SOURCED: reference years 2022-2026 on any leg, and the marketplace and listings leg in every year. THE 2025 ANCHOR THEREFORE STAYS GRADE C: every sourced leg stops at reference year 2021 and nothing free reaches the anchor year. RAIL: MAGNA media-owner advertising revenue, $398B for 2025 (digital pure players $294B + traditional media owners $104B, which sums exactly, so DIRECT MAIL IS OUT of this rail). All four pools are defined ex-direct-mail to match, which is the fix for the mechanical residual depression the era-7 verifier flagged: the superseded residual was computed with direct mail excluded from the denominator but present in two subtracted pools. RAIL SENSITIVITY EXCEEDS EVERY INTERVAL IN THIS SPLIT: IRS SOI corporate advertising deductions read $473,153m for 2022 against MAGNA's $325,000m, a $148B wedge that is overwhelmingly direct-response and retail money. Any chart of this split must name its rail in the axis label, not the footnote. || AGGREGATION: median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 1.9, reference-class 3.4, decomposition 2.5). No extremizing. Three routes, each run by all three lenses. || ROUTE C-A, decomposition of IAB's 'Other' bucket ($12.5B in FY2025) using its own last-published internal composition, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.45. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: BUCKET COMPOSITION BREAK - digital audio left 'Other' after FY2021 and directories were named into it from FY2022, so the FY2021 shares cannot be applied to the FY2025 total directly and the raw series must never be read across that join. TIME DRIFT - lead generation grew with the performance market while classified listing revenue migrated to transaction fees, so classifieds' share of the classified-plus-lead-generation pair falls; the lenses set it at 45, 55 and about 64 percent, and that single parameter is where the lens spread lives. || ROUTE C-B, Census SAS print legs extrapolated past their discontinuation, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.30. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENT: extrapolation across four to five unpublished reference years at each leg's own observed compound rate (newspaper classified -10 to -11 percent a year, directories -13.6 to -15 percent a year), with the print-only portion of the directory line separated from the digital portion already counted in C-A. The route's INPUTS are grade A to 2021; only the carry-forward is C. || ROUTE C-C, marketplace and listings leg rebuilt bottom-up from EDGAR and company disclosure, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.25. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: LISTED-COMPANY BIAS - EDGAR filers over-represent consolidated national portals and miss private and regional portals, direction up 8 to 15 percent; DEFINITIONAL BIAS the other way - Zillow Premier Agent, Angi and LinkedIn Recruiter seats are arguably lead generation or service fees rather than listing advertisements, direction down 10 to 15 percent; the two roughly cancel, so the central is not shifted and the interval is widened instead. De-duplicated against C-A, because roughly $3.5-7B of the listings revenue is already inside IAB's 'Other'. || INTERVAL: min lower to max upper across the lenses. WARNING, and it is a scope statement rather than an uncertainty band: above about 2.8 percent of the market (about $11.1B) the interval is FRAME, not measurement error, because two lenses set their upper bound on a widened denominator that counts the listings successors ($410-421B rather than $398B). The in-frame-only interval is 1.4 to 2.8 percent, i.e. $5.6B to $11.1B. The two readings are both correct on their own frames and must never be blended in a chart. || SCOPE ALTERNATIVE, recorded because it is the era's boundary-shift argument in one number: on a listings-inclusive reading the classified money type is about $21B (range $15-29B), of which roughly $12-16B sits outside every published US advertising total. Indeed's US revenue alone ($5.31B) approaches the whole of IAB's $12.5B 'Other' bucket. || DEFINITIONAL FORK 1: lead generation is roughly $4.5-6B of IAB's 'Other'. Two lenses move it to direct response on the ground that money paid per acquired lead is action-priced; one keeps a portion at weight 0.35 on the ground that a firm paying per lead for a roofer is buying what the classified page sold. That call produces almost the whole 1.9-to-3.4 spread. DEFINITIONAL FORK 2: directory money is carried in classified here, following the record, the hunt and IAB's own bucket; the alternative moves this pool from 2.5 to about 2.2 percent in 2025 but from 9.3 to about 5.2 percent in 2008.

direct_response.statement: National direct-response buyers - advertisers paying for a measurable action rather than for reach - account for about 38.0 percent of US advertising spend in 2025, roughly $151.2B, dominated by national search, commerce and retail media and performance social. Direct mail sits outside this rail on both sides of the ledger.
direct_response.unit: percent of US advertising spend, 2025 (MAGNA media-owner rail, $398B, direct mail excluded)
direct_response.method: SOURCED BY: POOL NOT SOURCED; ONE INPUT SOURCED AT GRADE A. IAB/PwC's 'Revenues by pricing model' exhibit publishes the performance-priced share of US digital annually 2004-2019 - 57 percent for 2008, 62-66 percent across 2010-2019, 62.1 percent at HY2019 - which converts 'two-thirds of digital is performance-priced' from an assumption into a published number for twelve of the nineteen era years. The exhibit was discontinued after HY2019, so 2020-2026 is EXTRAPOLATION. The only source that ever sized the whole pool, DMA/IHS Global Insight ($153.3B in 2010, 54.2 percent of US ad expenditure), died inside the era. Pool grade C. RAIL: MAGNA media-owner advertising revenue, $398B for 2025 (digital pure players $294B + traditional media owners $104B, which sums exactly, so DIRECT MAIL IS OUT of this rail). All four pools are defined ex-direct-mail to match, which is the fix for the mechanical residual depression the era-7 verifier flagged: the superseded residual was computed with direct mail excluded from the denominator but present in two subtracted pools. RAIL SENSITIVITY EXCEEDS EVERY INTERVAL IN THIS SPLIT: IRS SOI corporate advertising deductions read $473,153m for 2022 against MAGNA's $325,000m, a $148B wedge that is overwhelmingly direct-response and retail money. Any chart of this split must name its rail in the axis label, not the footnote. || AGGREGATION: median of three lens centrals (structural-proxy 38.0, reference-class 36.5, decomposition 40.7). No extremizing. THE APPARENT AGREEMENT IS AN ARTEFACT: all three centrals are three parameterisations of ONE unobserved quantity, the performance-priced share of US digital in 2025, which the lenses set at 60.0, 62.6 and 67.7 percent. Their 4.2pp dispersion measures disagreement about one parameter, not independent convergence, which is why the interval is taken from the combined lens bounds and not from the dispersion. || ROUTE D-A, performance-priced share applied to IAB's mutually exclusive FY2025 format partition, then strip local-bought digital and add national traditional direct response, MEDIAN WEIGHT 0.50. All three lenses run this route, and one lens's two variants (mix-shift decomposition of the 2019-2025 increment versus direct format weighting) are near-duplicates of each other because both consume the same IAB partition and the same HY2019 anchor - that is one route, not two. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: pricing basis is not buyer intent, with offsetting errors in both directions netting small; local-bought digital is removed so the pools stay disjoint; and the load-bearing step is extrapolating IAB's published 62.1 percent across the five unmeasured years that contain Performance Max, Advantage+ and the rise of retail media. || ROUTE D-B, the DMA/IHS direct-marketing pool decayed forward and rail-converted, WEIGHT 0.45 in the lens that ran it. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: DMA's denominator sits on a billings and deductions rail rather than a media-owner rail, and is converted at IRS SOI / MAGNA 2022 = 1.456; DMA's pool includes local direct marketing and lead generation, so the national portion is taken at 65 percent; the 2010 share of 54.2 percent is carried UP to about 62 percent for search, retail media and performance social growth. This route shares no input with D-A - different compiler, different decade, different rail - and lands at 37.6 percent against D-A's 38.5 percent. THE ONE GENUINELY INDEPENDENT CONVERGENCE IN THE ERA. || ROUTE D-C, advertiser-stated performance share (WARC/Ebiquity), WEIGHT 0.00 to 0.20, bound only. PROXY-POPULATION-GAP ADJUSTMENTS: global to US, +2 to +4pp; large-advertiser panel to whole market, +5 to +10pp; the survey conflates 'performance' as short-term activation intent with 'direct response' as measurable-action pricing. Adjusted it reads 44 to 57 percent and sets the top of the interval. || NEAR-DUPLICATE DECLARED AND DISCOUNTED: the seller-filings route (Alphabet, Meta and Amazon 10-Ks) is not independent of D-A, because Amazon's sponsored-product revenue sits inside IAB's search line, so it re-counts what D-A counts once. || RETIRED: the superseded path (b) - search plus commerce media plus 70 percent of social - is not a route. SELLERS.summary: The seller side concentrated, then re-concentrated around a third pole. Google, Meta and Amazon took roughly 61% of US digital ad spend in 2025 (Google ~25.6%, Meta ~21.3%, Amazon ~13.9% on eMarketer's counts), and the top ten sellers took 84.1% of all US internet ad revenue, up from 78.6% in 2021 - the open web's share shrank every year of the era. In absolute terms Google advertising revenue was $294.7B in 2025, Meta's $196.2B and Amazon's advertising services $68.6B. Amazon is the structural novelty: retail media turned every large retailer into a media owner selling its own shelf, and it did so by converting trade-promotion and co-op money into auction inventory. The intermediary cut stayed contested all era. Google's own 2020 disclosure said publishers keep about 69 cents of an advertiser dollar when both ends of the trade are Google; the DOJ said Google keeps at least 35 cents of every open-web display dollar and that AdX had held a 20% take rate since 2009 while rivals charged closer to 10%. Two courts agreed the concentration was unlawful: Judge Mehta held on 2024-08-05 that Google monopolised general search and general search text advertising, and Judge Brinkema held on 2025-04-17 that it monopolised the open-web publisher ad server and ad exchange markets and unlawfully tied them. Distribution stayed the other half of the story: Google paid $26.3B in default revenue share in 2021 and $59.9B in total traffic acquisition costs in 2025, a 20.3% TAC rate.

MEDIUM.summary: The era opens with the internet as one medium among many and closes with it as the market. US internet ad revenue went from $23.4B in 2008 to $294.6B in 2025 - a 12.6x rise, and the only down year in the whole run was 2009 (-3%). Digital was roughly 72% of all US ad spend by 2025. Inside digital, the medium that moved was mobile: about 66% of US digital dollars went to mobile placements in 2025, a share that has held near two-thirds since 2024, and it was mobile that carried search volume to Google's disclosed 5 trillion queries a year. The 2025 format split was search $114.2B (38.8%), display $81.6B, digital video $78.0B, digital audio $8.4B and 'other' - classifieds, directories and lead generation - $12.5B (4.2%). Social alone was $117.7B and commerce media $63.4B. CTV, at roughly $33B, became the channel where brand television money finally crossed into an auction. Meanwhile the tracked legacy channels kept shrinking on schedule: PwC's outlook has US TV advertising down 13.4% in 2025 and newspapers plus consumer magazines down 3.5%; directory advertising fell from a $14.7B peak in 2005 to roughly $1.1B in 2024; USPS Marketing Mail volume fell from 99 billion pieces in FY2008 to 56.8 billion in FY2025. Classifieds, directories and direct mail did not disappear in era 7 - they were re-platformed, and the money that used to buy a line of type now buys an impression in an auction.

SCALE.summary: US advertising spend ran from roughly $270-280B at the era's start to roughly $400-420B in 2025, depending on whose definition you take: MAGNA puts 2025 US media-owner ad revenue at $398B, eMarketer at $422B, and the two are not measuring the same universe. Against a nominal US GDP of $30.76T that is about 1.3% of GDP - materially below the 2.0% that the Coen/McCann series recorded for 2007 and far below the 2.3-2.4% that the same series and IRS data recorded at the 2000 peak. This is the era's most important and most contested number: measured US advertising intensity fell while the platforms that supposedly captured advertising grew, which is why Silk and Berndt (NBER WP 28161) frame the question as 'a growth problem, a measurement problem, or both'. Part of the answer is a boundary problem: much of what Google, Meta and Amazon sell was money that older series never counted as advertising at all - Yellow Pages listings, classified lineage, co-op and trade allowances, catalogue and lead-generation spend. Globally, 2025 estimates diverge just as sharply: MAGNA says $979B, WPP Media says $1.14T. National brand and direct response cannot be ranked against each other; classified is unambiguously the smallest. PRICING.summary: This is the era in which the auction that defined era 6 died three times over. First, header bidding (2014-15, standardised by Prebid.js out of AppNexus) broke the waterfall: instead of calling exchanges in a fixed priority order, publishers made every exchange bid at once, which destroyed the sequential price discrimination the waterfall depended on and forced Google's ad server to compete on price. Second, on 2019-09-05 Google finished moving Ad Manager to a unified first-price auction, formally ending second-price for open-web display; bidders responded with bid shading, so the price is now set by the buyer's model rather than by the runner-up's bid. Third, the DOJ search trial and the Mehta opinion exposed what had replaced GSP on the search side: three 'pricing knobs' Google internally called 'intentional pricing' - squashing (launched as 'Butternut Squash'), format pricing, and rGSP, the randomized generalized second-price auction launched in 2019. Format pricing alone had grown to about 20% of Google's text-ads revenue per thousand queries before rGSP replaced it because rGSP made more money; rGSP raised top-slot CPCs by about 5.9% on desktop and 4.9% on mobile in pre-launch tests, advertisers cannot opt out, and Jerry Dischler testified that Google moved prices around 5% on average, up to 10% on some queries, to hit quarterly revenue targets - without telling advertisers. The intermediary take stayed opaque: ISBA/PwC found only 51% of advertiser programmatic spend reached the publisher with a 15% 'unknown delta', the ANA found about 36 cents of each DSP dollar reaching a consumer, Google's own 2020 disclosure said publishers keep about 69 cents when both ends are Google, and the DOJ said AdX had held a 20% take rate since 2009. Agency compensation completed its own long slide from commission to fee to principal media - the agency buying inventory as principal and reselling at an undisclosed markup - after the ANA/K2 rebate report of 2016.

MEASUREMENT.summary: Era 7 is where the century-old rule that a third party counts the audience finally broke. From ABC in 1914 to MRC accreditation after 1964, the market's discipline was that the buyer could audit someone other than the seller. In this era the same company sold the inventory, ran the auction, counted the impressions and attributed the conversions - and the failures were exactly what that arrangement predicts. Facebook admitted in 2016 that it had overstated average video view time for about two years by excluding views under three seconds, a method that plaintiffs said inflated the metric by up to 900%, and paid $40M in 2019 to settle the advertiser class action. The counting institutions that remained came under the same strain from the other side: the MRC stripped Nielsen's national and local TV accreditation in September 2021 after finding pandemic-era undercounts of 2-6%, which the VAB valued at least $468M of lost national ad revenue, and did not restore it until April 2023, nineteen months later. Programmatic added its own counting crisis: made-for-advertising sites, unmeasurable impressions and invalid traffic absorbed a large share of open-web spend, and by 2026 the IAB reported that bots make up over half of global web traffic with nearly 40% classified as malicious. Privacy shocks then removed the signals attribution ran on, so the buy side retreated to older, coarser instruments - media mix modelling and incrementality tests - which is a measurement regime change, not a tooling preference. Who paid the counter is the era's quiet answer: increasingly the seller, or nobody.

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era ran a full arc: from the finest-grained individual tracking ever built, through two deliberate signal amputations, to a coarser but far more powerful statistical regime run by the seller's model. The opening state was the third-party cookie and the mobile advertising ID, stitched by data brokers into cross-site profiles and priced impression by impression in real time. GDPR (2018-05-25) and California's CCPA (2020) imposed consent, and the measured effects were real but modest and contested - one publisher study found a 2.1% fall in click-through and 5.7% in revenue per click, another found roughly 10% falls in recorded page views and revenue, and a 2019 publisher survey found no aggregate programmatic decline at all. Apple's App Tracking Transparency (iOS 14.5, 2021-04-26) was the larger shock because it was a platform rule rather than a law: opt-in ran about 16% at launch rising to roughly 25% by mid-2022, and Meta told investors ATT was a headwind 'on the order of $10 billion' in 2022. Google's third-party cookie deprecation, announced in January 2020, was delayed three times, abandoned as a unilateral deprecation in July 2024, and stripped of even its choice prompt in April 2025 - so the cookie outlived the decade of preparation for its death. What replaced explicit targeting was implicit targeting: the advertiser stopped choosing the audience. Performance Max and Advantage+ take a goal and a feed; about 71% of Google advertisers ran Performance Max by 2025 and Meta's automated ad products ran at roughly a $60B annual rate. The era closes with targeting moving inside the conversation itself: Meta began using Meta AI chat interactions for ad targeting on 2025-12-16 with no opt-out, and OpenAI began serving contextual ads inside ChatGPT in February 2026.

events.title: Google completes its $3.1B acquisition of DoubleClick
events.desc: After eleven months of review, the European Commission cleared the deal and Google took control of DoubleClick the same day. It gave Google the publisher ad server (DFP) and the display plumbing that would become the ad exchange - the asset at the centre of the ad-tech monopolisation ruling seventeen years later.

events.title: Header bidding breaks the waterfall
events.desc: Publishers began running a parallel auction in the page header before calling the ad server, so every exchange bid at once instead of in a fixed priority order. Prebid.js, created in early 2015 by Matt Kendall and Paul Yang at AppNexus with Nick Jacob of Aplus, standardised the technique; AdExchanger's 2015 piece 'The Rise of Header Bidding and the End of the Publisher Waterfall' is the trade-press marker. The waterfall's sequential price discrimination was over, and Google's ad server had to compete on price.

events.title: GDPR takes effect
events.desc: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation imposed a consent requirement on the data collection that behavioural targeting ran on, and made consent management platforms a standard layer of the web. California's CCPA followed in 2020. Measured revenue effects on publishers were smaller than forecast and remain contested, but the compliance layer became permanent.

events.title: Google Ad Manager completes the move to a unified first-price auction
events.desc: Announced in March 2019, tested from 10 June on 1% of Ad Exchange traffic, and rolled out in full from early September, the change ended second-price pricing for Google's open-web display exchange and folded publisher price floors into unified pricing rules. Buyers responded with bid shading, so the clearing price became a function of the buyer's model rather than of the runner-up's bid.

events.title: Apple ships App Tracking Transparency in iOS 14.5
events.desc: Apps had to ask permission before tracking users across other companies' apps and websites. Opt-in ran around 16% at launch. It was a platform rule, not a law, and it cost the largest buyer of mobile signal more than any privacy statute had.

revenue_per_unit.statement: Google earned roughly 3.7 cents of advertising revenue per search query in 2025.
revenue_per_unit.unit: USD of advertising revenue per Google search query, 2025
revenue_per_unit.method: Google Search & other revenue was $224,532M in FY2025 (Alphabet 10-K, grade A). Google disclosed 'more than 5 trillion searches on Google annually' in March 2025 (grade A company statement); query volume grew through 2025, so the denominator is taken as 5.0-5.6 trillion. Search & other also contains Gmail, Maps and Play revenue, so a 10-15% haircut is applied to isolate core Search: $195B / 5.3T = $0.037. Bounds combine the no-haircut case at 5.0T ($0.045) and the full-haircut case at 5.6T ($0.033), widened for the disclosure's imprecision. Note that this is a global average; the US per-query figure is higher, since the US contributes 48% of Alphabet revenue on a far smaller share of world queries.

cost_to_serve.statement: In 2020 the direct cost of operating Google's search engine and its search ads business worked out to roughly 0.65 cents per query ($19.5B over ~3.0T queries), while the search default payments the court found for 2021 ($26.3B over ~3.3T queries) worked out to roughly 0.8 cents - Google paid more per query to be found than it spent answering it. On FY2025 figures the distribution cost per query is about 0.8-0.9 cents.
cost_to_serve.unit: USD of direct operating cost per Google search query
cost_to_serve.method: Cost numerator from findings of fact: in 2020 Google spent $8.4B operating its search engine (excluding revenue-share payments) and $11.1B operating its search ads business, a combined $19.5B (US v. Google, Mem. Op., FOF paras 52, 55; grade A). Query denominator interpolated log-linearly between Google's two official disclosures - 'more than 2 trillion' queries per year in 2016 and 'more than 5 trillion' in March 2025 - which implies 10.7% annual growth and about 3.0 trillion queries in 2020. $19.5B / 3.0T = $0.0065. Interval spans a 2.2-4.0T denominator. The distribution comparison uses FY2025 TAC of $59,926M at a 20.3% rate; applying that rate to Search & other revenue gives about $45B, divided by 5.0-5.6T queries = $0.008-0.009.

comparison_series.statement: In 2023 the cheapest generally available model of GPT-4 quality cost about 4.8 cents to produce one answer, roughly the entire advertising revenue of a Google search query.
comparison_series.unit: USD of inference cost per AI-generated answer, 2023
comparison_series.method: Standard answer defined as 1,000 input tokens plus 300 output tokens - a grounded, search-style response. GPT-4's list price - $30 per million input tokens and $60 per million output tokens at its March 2023 launch, unchanged at its July 2023 general availability - gives: (1,000/1e6 x $30) + (300/1e6 x $60) = $0.030 + $0.018 = $0.048. Cross-check on serving cost rather than list price: SemiAnalysis estimated ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 class) cost about 0.36 cents per query in early 2023 at roughly $694k/day, an order of magnitude below the GPT-4 list price - list price and marginal serving cost differ by roughly 10x, which the interval does not attempt to bridge.

comparison_series.statement: As of mid-2026 the cheap tier had stopped falling and had begun to tick back up: the cheapest model on Google's public price list cost about 0.022 cents for the same answer, up from about 0.0165 cents in 2025, because Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite was shut down on 1 June 2026 and every cheap tier launched since is priced above the old floor. Frontier reasoning models pushed per-answer cost up much further, because they emit far more tokens per answer than the fixed-length assumption allows.
comparison_series.unit: USD list-price cost of a fixed 1,000-in / 300-out answer at the cheapest generally available model at or above GPT-4 capability, 2026-06-30 freeze
comparison_series.method: Same 1,000-in / 300-out bundle. Cheapest model on Google's live Gemini price list at the 2026-06-30 freeze, verified again on 2026-07-31, is Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite at $0.10/$0.40 per million: $0.00022. The 'stopped falling' finding is evidenced by the price list, NOT by equality with the 2025 central: Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite ($0.075/$0.30 = $0.000165) was deprecated and shut down on 1 June 2026, and every cheap tier launched after it is dearer — Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite $0.25/$1.50 = $0.0007, GPT-5.4 Nano (17 March 2026) $0.20/$1.25 = $0.000575 against GPT-5 nano's $0.00017. Interval measures model selection across vendors: floor Amazon Nova Micro $0.000077 if still generally available at the freeze, ceiling GPT-5.4 Nano $0.000575. Frontier comparator is carried as a SEPARATE declared series and is restated on the July 2026 OpenAI list — GPT-5.4 Standard $2.50/$15 = $0.007 and GPT-5.5 $5/$30 = $0.014 — because the GPT-5.2 figure previously used ($1.75/$14 = $0.00595) is not on OpenAI's current price list and understates the frontier. The material caveat is that reasoning models generate several thousand output tokens per answer rather than 300, so a like-for-like answer at the frontier now costs 10-30x this figure; the fixed-token definition is held constant across the series so the four points remain comparable. Directional conclusion for P3, computed against the corrected 3.7 cents of ad revenue per query (e7-unit_econ-001): the floor cost of one machine-written answer is now roughly 0.6% of the advertising revenue of one search query, against roughly 130% of it in 2023.

boundary_notes: SHARED WITH ERA 6 (2002-2008). (1) The era boundary is a real data seam, not just a date. The Coen/McCann Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset - the only continuous US by-medium series - ends with 2007, at $279.6B of total US ad spend and 2.0% of GDP. Era 7 therefore runs on IAB/PwC for the digital half (continuous 1996-2025) and MAGNA/eMarketer for the all-media total, which are not definitionally identical to Coen. R2 must carry a concordance entry for the 2007/2008 splice and grade spliced years C. (2) Era 6 should close with US internet ad revenue at $21,206M for 2007; era 7 opens at $23,448M for 2008 (IAB/PwC, same series, so the two eras must agree exactly on these two numbers). (3) Google completed the DoubleClick acquisition on 2008-03-11 - announced April 2007 (era 6), closed in era 7. Era 6 should record the announcement, era 7 the close. (4) The quality-weighted second-price auction (GSP) that era 6 owns is the thing era 7 kills; era 6 should not claim GSP survived, and era 7 does not re-explain how GSP was built. (5) Google's ad-tech take rate and the AdX 20% fee both date from 2009 per the DOJ - inside era 7, not era 6. SHARED WITH P3 (post-freeze). Out-of-scope pointers, deliberately excluded from every claim: Judge Brinkema had not issued a remedies order in the ad-tech case as of the 2026-06-30 freeze (liability 2025-04-17, remedies trial September 2025, closing arguments concluded, opinion pending); OpenAI's ChatGPT ad pilot was US-only at the freeze with announced plans to expand; appeals of both the Mehta and Brinkema rulings were expected and unresolved. CONTESTED THREAD FOR THE CAPTURE CHAPTER. Measured US ad spend fell from about 2.3-2.4% of GDP in 2000 and 2.0% in 2007 to about 1.3% in 2025 while the platforms grew - so 'Google captured the ad market' cannot be asserted from the aggregate series alone. Silk & Berndt (NBER WP 28161) treat this as an open question. Era 7's own evidence favours a boundary-shift reading: a large share of platform revenue is money older series never counted as advertising (directory listings, classified lineage, co-op and trade allowances, lead generation), which is exactly why this record carries a rebuilt money-type split rather than a published one. (R3 verdict application) Claim e7-medium-003 - 'mobile took about 72% of US digital ad spending in 2025' - was REJECTED in adversarial verification: the cited EMARKETER piece reports 65.8% for 2024 and forecasts stability near two-thirds through 2028, and the 72% figure traced only to an SEO statistics aggregator. It is replaced at the same id by the 66% EMARKETER-sourced figure, the SQ Magazine citation is dropped, and the MEDIUM summary was rewritten to match. Note that 72 is also this record's figure for digital's share of TOTAL US ad spend (e7-medium-002), which is consistent with a transcription error rather than a finding.
